monsters.name: Laundry Hydra
monsters.chore: Fold a full basket of clean clothes
monsters.lore:
Adventurer, your neglect has summoned the Hydra from the hamper's abyss.

By abandoning the sweat-soaked fibers of your daily toil to the humid dark of the laundry pile, you have cultivated a mycological nightmare. Each discarded garment — heavy with sebum, shed keratin, and the salty ghosts of exertion — became a banquet for dermatophytes and opportunistic bacilli. The cotton and synthetic weaves, swollen with moisture, now host dense biofilms of *Staphylococcus epidermidis* and *Corynebacterium*, metabolizing your lipids into volatile short-chain fatty acids: isovaleric, propionic, butyric — the unmistakable perfume of forgotten socks.

As oxygen-starved pockets deepen between the layers, obligate anaerobes take the throne. *Clostridium* and *Peptostreptococcus* ferment amino acids into putrescine and cadaverine, while *Aspergillus* and *Penicilious* spores — ever-present in household dust — germinate hyphae that penetrate the fabric matrix, secreting cellulases and proteases that hydrolyze the very threads into assimilable sugars.

But the true horror stirs in the microscopic: *Dermatophagoides* — dust mites by the millions — graze upon the fungal-digested skin scales, their fecal pellets (rich in Der p 1 protease allergens) raining down into the weave. Each disturbance of the pile launches allergen clouds; each hour of delay thickens the biofilm mattress.

Now, the biomass has achieved critical cohesion. The sodden mass heaves. From the collar of a shirt, a neck extends — then another, and another — each head crowned with a ruff of lint and mold sporulation. The Laundry Hydra has awakened, hungry for the warmth of a living wearer.

Seize the basket. Deploy the detergent. The spin cycle awaits.

monsters.name: Trash Mimic
monsters.chore: Take out the overflowing kitchen trash
monsters.lore:
Adventurer, your refusal to tie the bag has birthed a mimic in the midden.

The overflowing bin is no mere receptacle — it is a bioreactor of staggering complexity. Vegetable peels, meat trimmings, dairy curds, and carbohydrate sludge mingle in a leachate soup where *Enterobacteriaceae* and *Lactobacillus* wage lactic-acid war, dropping the pH to levels that pickle the very plastic liner. Ethanol and acetic acid vaporize in the headspace; meanwhile, deep in the anaerobic core, methanogenic archaea — *Methanosaeta*, *Methanosarcina* — reduce acetate and CO₂ into methane, pressurizing the bag like a slow bomb.

Plastic does not escape unscathed. Phthalates (DEHP, DINP) and bisphenol analogs leach from the liner into the acidic broth, plasticizing the polymer while disrupting the endocrine ambitions of any organism foolish enough to linger. Microfragments, abraded by settling waste, suspend as colloidal shards — vectors for biofilm attachment.

The entomological complement is no less baroque. *Drosophila melanogaster* lays clutches in the fermenting fruit; *Musca domestica* deposits eggs that hatch into maggots secreting digestive liquefaction enzymes, accelerating the rot. *Blattella germanica* nymphs forage the rim, their cuticles acquiring antibiotic-resistant *Enterococcus* from the filth. Phorid flies breed in the slime layer coating the bin's interior — a living carpet of extracellular polymeric substance.

And now, the mimicry completes. The bag itself *moves* — the plastic rippling as gas pockets shift beneath a unified biomass that has learned the shape of discarded takeout containers. A false lid yawns open, revealing teeth of calcified coffee grounds and eggshell shards. The Trash Mimic inhales the miasma of skatole, indole, and hydrogen sulfide — and exhales a challenge.

Grasp the knot. Haul it to the curb. The truck comes Tuesday.
